checks.prompt: Three requirements land on a team. (a) A tutor bot that must recall a learner's goals and progress weeks later, updating them as they change. (b) Question answering over a fixed 800-page policy manual that never changes. (c) Summarising one long contract in a single call. Which one is this approach for, and what is the reframing that makes it work?
checks.explanation: The insight is an analogy to virtual memory: give the model a small fast working memory that is always in context and a large slow external store, and let the agent page between them using tool calls, so a finite window behaves like unbounded persistent memory. That is aimed squarely at state that EVOLVES across turns and sessions. A static corpus is retrieval's job, and something that fits in one call needs neither — using this for one big static document is explicitly the wrong tool.
options: (a). The reframing is to treat a finite context window as a memory-management problem, borrowing the operating system's virtual-memory trick: a small always-present working memory plus large external storage, with the AGENT itself deciding what to page in and out through tool calls. (b) is a static corpus, which retrieval alone serves, and (c) fits in one call, where a long-context model is simplest
(b). The approach is a retrieval layer over documents, so a large static corpus is its strongest case; evolving conversational state is better handled by a longer context window
(c). Its purpose is extending a single call over a document too large for the window, by paging sections of that document through the context
All three, since any task benefits from unbounded memory and the external store subsumes both retrieval and long context

checks.prompt: Lay out the operating-system analogy this design is built on, mapping at least four operating-system concepts onto their equivalents here. Then explain the move the notebook calls defining — what makes it unusual compared with an ordinary framework's conversation memory — and describe the three tiers of storage, saying which is in context and which is not.
checks.expected: A correct answer must map the analogy with at least four correspondences: fast, small, expensive memory corresponds to the context window — the system prompt, the memory blocks, the recent messages and the tool definitions; slow, huge, cheap storage corresponds to the external stores; a process issuing system calls corresponds to the agent invoking its memory-editing tools; a page fault that loads from storage corresponds to a search that pulls an old fact back into context; and eviction when memory is full corresponds to summarising or moving overflow out to external storage. The defining move must be named as self-editing memory: when the user reveals a durable fact, the agent does not merely reply — it CALLS a function to write that fact into its always-in-context memory, so it persists into every future turn. What makes this unusual is that the model is both the consumer of memory and its manager, deciding what is worth keeping, rather than a framework silently truncating or summarising a buffer on its behalf. The three tiers must be distinguished: a small, always-in-context, editable working memory of labelled size-limited blocks — canonically one describing the agent itself and one describing the user; a searchable log of the complete conversation history that is kept OUT of context and paged in on demand; and an unbounded external store of arbitrary facts, searched semantically. Only the first is in context. Noting that a tool call can request another reasoning step, so the agent can read, think and write within one turn, or that blocks are size-limited and can be shared between agents, is a plus.

checks.prompt: A team's agent is behaving oddly: its answers have become vague and it seems to have less room for the actual conversation. Inspecting it, they find its always-in-context blocks now hold a long history of everything the user has ever mentioned, because their prompt tells the agent to save anything that might matter. What is the diagnosis and what should have gone where?
checks.explanation: The always-in-context tier is small on purpose, because everything in it is paid for on every single turn and competes with the conversation for room. So the discipline is editorial: keep only durable, high-value facts there — the agent's own persona and a compact picture of the user — and put everything else in the unbounded external store, which is searched on demand and costs nothing until it is needed. The complete conversation is separately logged out of context and can be searched, so saving it into the blocks is duplicating something already recoverable.
options: The always-in-context tier is deliberately tiny, and stuffing it crowds out the conversation itself — that is the cost being paid for the vagueness. Only durable, high-value facts belong there: who the agent is, and the small set of stable things it knows about the user. Everything else belongs in the unbounded external store, retrieved on demand, or is already recoverable from the searchable conversation log
The blocks have no size limit by design, so the problem is the model losing attention over a long block; the fix is to reorder the blocks so recent facts appear first
The blocks are correct and the problem is the external store being unused; moving conversation history into it would free context because the store is also always in context
The agent should not be editing memory at all — memory management belongs to the framework, and the prompt should be changed to stop it calling the memory tools

checks.prompt: Implement the memory hierarchy. Define `MemoryOverflow(ValueError)` and `MemoryBlock(label, value="", limit=200)` with `append(text)`, which commits `value + "\n" + text` stripped, and `replace(old, new)`, which raises `ValueError` if `old` is not in the current value and otherwise commits the substituted string. A commit longer than `limit` characters raises `MemoryOverflow` naming the label, the length, the limit and the word `"archival"`, and MUST leave the block unchanged. Define `Agent(blocks=None, limit=200)` building a `core` dict of `MemoryBlock`s from a label-to-value mapping, plus an empty `archival` list and an empty `recall` list. Give it `core_memory_append(label, text)` and `core_memory_replace(label, old, new)` delegating to the block (an unknown label raising `KeyError`); `archival_memory_insert(text)`; `archival_memory_search(query, k=2)`, returning the `k` stored strings sharing the most lowercase whitespace-split words with the query, most first, ties by insertion order, excluding any with no shared word; `message(role, content)`, appending `{"role", "content"}` to `recall` and nothing else; `conversation_search(query, k=2)`, the same ranking over `recall` and returning those entries; `remember(label, text)`, which appends to the core block and returns `"core"`, or on overflow inserts the text into the archival store and returns `"archival"`; and `context_window()`, returning one `"[label] value"` line per core block, in insertion order, joined by newlines. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The assertion to dwell on is that the block is byte-identical after a rejected write. Enforcing the budget atomically is what makes the whole scheme workable: a refused edit is not a corrupted block, it is a signal, and the eviction policy is built directly on it — try the small fast tier, and on refusal put the value in the unbounded store, with the context window intact either way. Note what else the refusals buy. An edit against text that is not present is rejected rather than silently doing nothing, which is how a hallucinated edit gets caught. And notice the separation in the last blocks: sixty messages go into the conversation log, the context window does not change by a single character, and the message from thirty turns ago is still findable by search. That is the page fault — the fact was never in the window, and it did not need to be.
checks.test:
agent = Agent({"persona": "I am a patient coding tutor.", "human": ""}, limit=120)

# What the model sees every turn is the core blocks -- small, always present.
assert agent.context_window() == "[persona] I am a patient coding tutor.\n[human] "
agent.core_memory_append("human", "Name: Dana.")
agent.core_memory_append("human", "Goal: learning Rust.")
assert agent.core["human"].value == "Name: Dana.\nGoal: learning Rust."
assert "[human] Name: Dana." in agent.context_window()

# A fact that sharpens is edited in place rather than appended twice.
agent.core_memory_replace("human", "Goal: learning Rust.", "Goal: ship a CLI by Q3.")
assert agent.core["human"].value == "Name: Dana.\nGoal: ship a CLI by Q3."
assert "learning Rust" not in agent.context_window()

# An edit whose target is not there is refused -- a hallucinated edit must not
# silently do nothing.
before = agent.core["human"].value
try:
    agent.core_memory_replace("human", "Goal: learn Go.", "Goal: learn C.")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an edit against absent text must be refused")
assert agent.core["human"].value == before

# The budget is enforced, and enforcement is ATOMIC: the rejected write leaves the
# block exactly as it was, so the caller can spill to external storage instead.
before = agent.core["human"].value
try:
    agent.core_memory_append("human", "verbose backstory " * 20)
except MemoryOverflow as overflow:
    assert "human" in str(overflow) and "archival" in str(overflow), overflow
else:
    raise AssertionError("an over-budget write must be refused")
assert agent.core["human"].value == before, "the block must be unchanged"

# A replacement that grows past the budget is refused on the same terms.
try:
    agent.core_memory_replace("human", "Name: Dana.", "Name: " + "D" * 200)
except MemoryOverflow:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("a growing replacement must be refused")
assert agent.core["human"].value == before

# That refusal is what the eviction policy is built on: what fits stays in context,
# what does not goes to the unbounded store, and core is never damaged either way.
assert agent.remember("human", "UTC-6.") == "core"
assert "UTC-6." in agent.context_window()
kept = agent.core["human"].value
assert agent.remember("human", "a very long anecdote " * 20) == "archival"
assert agent.core["human"].value == kept
assert any("anecdote" in note for note in agent.archival)

# The external store is searched on demand and never sits in the context window.
for note in ["Dana prefers worked examples over theory.",
             "Dana works in timezone UTC-6.",
             "Dana finished the borrow-checker chapter.",
             "Dana hit a lifetime error in her argument parser."]:
    agent.archival_memory_insert(note)
hits = agent.archival_memory_search("lifetime borrow error", k=2)
assert hits[0] == "Dana hit a lifetime error in her argument parser.", hits
assert "Dana prefers worked examples over theory." not in hits, hits
assert len(agent.archival_memory_search("Dana", k=2)) == 2
assert agent.archival_memory_search("quantum chromodynamics") == []
assert agent.archival_memory_search("Dana", k=0) == []
assert all(note not in agent.context_window() for note in agent.archival)

# Ties keep insertion order, so search is deterministic.
plain = Agent({"human": ""})
for note in ["alpha beta", "alpha gamma", "delta"]:
    plain.archival_memory_insert(note)
assert plain.archival_memory_search("alpha", k=3) == ["alpha beta", "alpha gamma"]

# The full conversation is logged out of context and paged back in by searching --
# a message that scrolled away is still findable long after.
for turn in range(30):
    plain.message("user", f"message number {turn}")
plain.message("user", "my cat is called Mango")
for turn in range(30):
    plain.message("assistant", f"reply number {turn}")
assert len(plain.recall) == 61
assert plain.context_window() == "[human] "
found = plain.conversation_search("cat Mango", k=1)
assert found[0]["content"] == "my cat is called Mango", found
assert found[0]["role"] == "user", found

# Conversation and external store are separate: logging a turn writes nothing to
# core memory or to the archival store.
assert plain.core["human"].value == ""
assert plain.archival == ["alpha beta", "alpha gamma", "delta"]

# A block nobody created cannot be written to.
try:
    agent.core_memory_append("scratch", "x")
except KeyError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown block must be refused")

checks.prompt: A prototype works in demos but disappoints in production: the agent frequently fails to save facts it was told, an occasional lookup for something the user definitely said returns nothing, and the per-conversation cost and latency are far above the team's estimate based on a plain completion. What explains the three?
checks.explanation: Three independent realities. Saving is an action the model has to choose to take, so reliability tracks the model's function-calling ability — a weak model simply forgets, or claims an edit it did not make. Retrieval from the external store is semantic, so it is subject to phrasing and to the embedding model, and it will miss; it is not a structured query over a database. And the cost model is different from a plain completion by construction: each memory edit is another round trip, and chaining read-think-write within one turn multiplies both tokens and latency.
options: Memory does not manage itself: the agent only remembers if it is prompted and tooled to call the memory functions and the model is good enough at doing so — weaker models forget to save or fabricate edits. Lookups into the external store are semantic rather than exact, so phrasing and the embedding model decide what comes back and misses happen; it is not a substitute for a structured query. And every memory edit is an extra model round trip, with chained read-think-write steps multiplying tokens and latency over a plain completion
All three come from the block size limit being too small: raising it makes the agent save more reliably, keeps everything in context so no lookup is needed, and removes the extra round trips
The missing saves and missing lookups are the same bug — an unflushed write buffer — and the cost is the embedding model, which can be disabled without losing search
The agent is stateless between requests unless the same conversation identifier is reused, which explains all three symptoms; passing it consistently resolves them

checks.prompt: Compare this approach with three alternatives — a long-context model, plain retrieval over a static corpus, and a general agent framework's built-in conversation buffers — saying what each gives and when it wins. Then advise a team building a personal health-coaching assistant used daily for months, which must remember evolving goals and also answer from a fixed library of clinical guidance. Explain what you would use for which part and why the two are not the same problem.
checks.expected: A correct answer must characterise all three alternatives. A long-context model gives lossless recall within one large window and is the simplest thing that works when everything fits in a single call; its limits are that it resets every call, so nothing accumulates, and cost scales with the length of what you resend. Retrieval over a static corpus gives lookup into fixed documents and wins for question answering over material that does not change; the agent never WRITES anything, which is precisely what it does not cover. A framework's conversation buffers and summaries give lightweight history you wire yourself with full control, which is a reasonable fit if you already live in that framework and want simple history rather than self-editing persistent memory. This approach gives self-editing, persistent memory plus a stateful agent runtime, and wins when an assistant must remember a user or a task ACROSS sessions. The advice must split the health assistant along that line: the evolving goals, preferences and progress are accumulating, self-edited state and belong in this approach's memory tiers, whereas the fixed clinical library is a static corpus and should be served by retrieval. The reason they are not the same problem must be given: one requires the agent to write and revise what it knows over time, the other requires only reading from something that never changes — and conflating them leads to either stuffing a static corpus into memory or expecting retrieval to accumulate. A strong answer notes the two compose, since such an agent commonly runs retrieval over its own external store, and adds that the durable per-user state makes the agent a stateful server-side object with an identifier, which brings persistence, lifecycle and cleanup obligations of its own.
